summary: Enterprise frontend platform engineering, Lead React/TypeScript role, scalable component architecture and guardrailed AI product delivery

motivation_letter.name: Goonja Gandhi
paragraphs: Two details in this role stood out to me more than the title: the expectation that the lead frontend developer keeps looking for ways to make the platform simpler, not only faster, and the instruction to use AI in a structured way with guardrails. Together they describe a position that is as much about setting boundaries — what the codebase should do, what an AI feature is permitted to do — as about shipping features. Before I wrote software I studied linguistic philosophy, and the habit I kept from it is asking what problem an abstraction is actually solving. Guardrails are that question applied to a system: not whether a capability is impressive, but where its edges should be.

That question has shaped how I have worked. At Tata Consultancy Services I was a senior frontend developer directing a team of five, which meant architecture decisions, code review and frontend standards were the job itself rather than additions to it. The most useful change I made there was not visual: restructuring data flow with RxJS and TypeScript reduced API calls by 40%, and that only worked because the conversation with backend developers happened before implementation, not after. Later, on an accessibility-focused complaint resolution platform built with React, Redux and REST APIs, I raised WCAG compliance by 30% by treating accessibility as a constraint that shapes the component API rather than a review step at the end.

The work I do outside my job tends to follow the same instinct downward. My AI fact-verification project combined RAG with FAISS and LLM reasoning, but the lesson was architectural: retrieval is not reasoning, and collapsing them into one step produces confident wrong answers. Deciding what to cache, what to rate-limit and where a human should take over was the real design work. The performance side was similar in kind — code splitting and caching took the bundle from 941KB to under 300KB and Lighthouse from 73 to 95. Separately I built a small reactive JavaScript engine implementing useState-like reactivity, mainly to see what React's API is hiding. A lead does not need to have written a framework; it does change how you set standards, because you can tell which rules are load-bearing and which are simply habit.

What I would bring to this role is the habit of doing that in the open: writing frontend standards down so review stays fast and consistent, bringing backend developers into UI-driven API decisions early, and moving prototypes toward production rather than delivering demos that are rebuilt afterwards. I would want simplification to remain an ongoing activity rather than a single cleanup, and I am applying because the role asks for someone who can hold both frontend architecture and product judgement at the same time.
motivation_letter.closing: Thank you for considering my application. I look forward to the opportunity to discuss how I can contribute.
